items.topic: Cryptosporidium — soap-and-water hand hygiene; alcohol-based sanitizers not effective
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A community nurse teaches a household with confirmed cryptosporidiosis about hand hygiene. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water at key times; alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not effective against Cryptosporidium
Alcohol-based hand sanitizer alone is preferred after diaper changes because it kills Crypto oocysts
Hand hygiene is unnecessary once watery diarrhea begins
Only antibacterial soap with bleach must be used; plain soap and water never help

rationales.A: Correct. CDC Preventing Crypto and Merck Prevention: alcohol-based sanitizers are not effective against this parasite; soap-and-water handwashing at key times is recommended.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Alcohol-based sanitizers are not effective against Crypto (CDC/Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hand hygiene remains essential to limit fecal-oral spread.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Thorough soap-and-water handwashing is the recommended hygiene practice; bleach is not required for routine handwashing.

items.topic: NGN matrix — cryptosporidiosis prevention indicated vs not
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: For a family with a child recovering from cryptosporidiosis, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Wash hands with soap and water after toileting/diapering and before preparing food
Avoid swallowing untreated lake, river, or poorly treated recreational water
Rely only on alcohol-based hand sanitizer because it reliably kills Crypto oocysts

Tell contacts that Crypto never spreads person to person so hygiene is optional

rationales.R2: Indicated. Merck: do not swallow untreated recreational water; CDC advises avoiding contaminated water.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Alcohol-based sanitizers are not effective against Crypto.

rationales.R5: Not indicated. Person-to-person fecal-oral transmission occurs; stools are highly infectious (Merck).

items.topic: Legionnaires’ disease — inhale contaminated water mist; generally not person-to-person
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: During an outbreak investigation teaching session, which statement about Legionnaires’ disease transmission is most accurate?

options.text: People usually get it by breathing mist from water systems contaminated with Legionella; in general it is not spread person to person
It spreads mainly by casual skin contact, so gloves alone stop community outbreaks
It is almost always transmitted by coughing directly onto others in the same room
It only comes from spoiled food, never from building water systems

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: breathe mist containing Legionella; in general not person to person. Merck: acquired by inhaling aerosols of contaminated water; not transmitted person to person (rare probable exception).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Transmission is via aerosols/aspiration of contaminated water, not casual skin contact.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Person-to-person spread is not the usual route.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Building plumbing/water aerosols (showers, hot tubs, cooling towers) are classic sources.

items.topic: Fat embolism after long-bone fracture — dyspnea/hypoxemia and neurologic changes
items.stem: A client with a femoral fracture develops sudden shortness of breath and new confusion about 36 hours after injury. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?

options.text: Fat embolism syndrome related to long-bone fracture
Simple anxiety with no need to assess oxygenation
Delayed wound hematoma that never affects breathing
Benign muscle spasm that explains acute hypoxemia

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: fat embolism after long-bone fractures causes rapid-onset hypoxemia often with neurologic changes (and petechial rash). OpenStax: fat embolism risk after long-bone fractures; monitor for neurologic changes or shortness of breath, commonly 24–72 hours after fracture.
rationales.B: Incorrect. New dyspnea and confusion require urgent respiratory/neuro assessment for embolism.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hematoma does not explain acute dyspnea and confusion in this pattern.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Muscle spasm does not cause acute hypoxemic respiratory syndromes.

sources.title: Nonthrombotic Pulmonary Embolism
sources.evidence: Long-bone fractures can introduce fat into venous circulation; syndrome with severe hypoxemia, neurologic changes, petechial rash.

sources.evidence: Long-bone fractures increase fat embolism risk; monitor for neurologic changes or shortness of breath, often 24–72 hours after fracture.

items.topic: Hepatic encephalopathy — lactulose as standard treatment with cause correction
items.stem: A client with cirrhosis develops confusion and asterixis. Besides treating precipitating factors, which medication is commonly used for hepatic (portosystemic) encephalopathy?

options.text: Oral lactulose (often with a nonabsorbable antibiotic such as rifaximin as indicated)
High-dose intravenous insulin as first-line encephalopathy therapy
Routine thrombolysis for every episode of asterixis
Disulfiram to reverse ammonia-related confusion

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: treatment includes correcting the acute cause, oral lactulose, and nonabsorbable antibiotics such as rifaximin. OpenStax hepatic encephalopathy table lists lactulose (and antibiotics) among treatments.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Insulin is not first-line therapy for hepatic encephalopathy.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Thrombolysis is not the treatment for asterixis from encephalopathy.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Disulfiram is for alcohol aversion, not ammonia/encephalopathy treatment.

sources.title: Portosystemic Encephalopathy
sources.evidence: Treatment usually correction of acute cause, oral lactulose, and nonabsorbable antibiotics such as rifaximin.

items.topic: NGN matrix — hepatic encephalopathy care indicated vs not
items.stem: For a client with cirrhosis and new confusion with asterixis, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Administer ordered lactulose and monitor response (e.g., stooling/mental status per orders)
Help identify and treat precipitants such as infection, GI bleeding, dehydration, or electrolyte imbalance
Assess for asterixis and changes in cognition as encephalopathy cues

Give sedatives liberally because drowsiness always improves encephalopathy

rationales.R2: Indicated. Merck: acute episodes often precipitated by infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte issues, dehydration, sedatives.

rationales.R5: Not indicated. Sedatives/analgesics can precipitate encephalopathy (Merck).

items.topic: Testicular torsion — surgical emergency; urgent detorsion/surgery to salvage testis
items.stem: An adolescent presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea, and a high-riding tender testis. What is the priority nursing/medical action?

options.text: Treat as a surgical emergency—facilitate immediate evaluation for manual detorsion/urgent surgery to restore blood flow
Schedule elective outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks because torsion is never urgent
Apply ice and discharge home without provider notification
Start oral antibiotics alone and cancel any surgical consult

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: emergency; immediate manual detorsion followed by surgical intervention. MedlinePlus: surgery as soon as possible; salvage best if within about 6 hours.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delay risks permanent testicular damage.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Requires emergency evaluation, not home ice alone.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Antibiotics alone do not treat ischemia from torsion; surgery is needed.

sources.title: Testicular Torsion

items.topic: Assignment/delegation — verify competency (Right Person); staffing considers acuity and skill mix
items.stem: A charge nurse is assigning tasks on a busy unit. Which action best reflects safe leadership practice?

options.text: Assign/delegate only to staff with verified education and competency for the task, considering patient acuity and skill mix—not census alone
Give the most complex unstable clients to the least experienced float nurse without orientation or competency check
Ignore acuity and assign solely by alphabetical room numbers
Delegate nursing judgment and initial assessment to untrained assistive personnel

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Right Person: RN ensures required education/competencies. AHRQ: adequate staffing depends on acuity, skill mix, expertise—not numbers alone.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Unverified competency for complex unstable clients is unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Acuity and skill mix must inform assignments.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nursing process/judgment cannot be delegated (OpenStax principles).

sources.evidence: Staffing influenced by patient acuity, admissions/transfers, staff skill mix and expertise—not ratios alone.

items.jurisdiction_note: O. Reg. 799/93 under the Nursing Act lists directing inadequately trained/incompetent performance of nursing functions as professional misconduct; aligns with competency verification principles.
items.topic: Ontario — directing staff to perform functions beyond training/competence is professional misconduct
items.stem: An Ontario charge nurse knowingly assigns a nursing function to a team member who has not been trained or demonstrated competence for that function. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Directing a member/student/team member to perform nursing functions they are not adequately trained or competent to perform is professional misconduct under O. Reg. 799/93
Ontario regulations encourage assigning any task to anyone regardless of competence
Only the client can be disciplined for staff competency gaps
Training and competence never matter if the shift is short-staffed

rationales.A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 s.1 item 3 defines this directing as professional misconduct. OpenStax Right Person reinforces verifying education/competency before assigning/delegating.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The regulation prohibits directing inadequately trained/incompetent performance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Accountability for directing unsafe assignment rests with the directing nurse under the misconduct regulation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Staffing pressure does not authorize incompetent assignment.
